I never played the original aoe3 but I loved aoe2 and other RTS titles such as Blizzard's Craft games.
I was, however, let down by aoe4 and I cannot recommend that game to anyone. I heard lots of people say that aoe3 is the "black sheep" of the franchise so I avoided it for the longest time.

I played aoe4 for like ~10 hours and uninstalled it (it was laggy, boring, ugly and didn't seem to have that much polish)... I played aoe3 de for ~8 hours and I'm loving every second of it! I even bought all of the DLCs pretty much instantly.

So my take is: Even if you'd have disliked aoe4, do give aoe3 a shot. Don't mind all the negative stuff online. Some people don't like the Home City / Card system or the lack of resource drop-off points. Those never bothered me in this game. The campaign/story is way more interesting than in aoe4 and I think aoe3's story might even be better than aoe2's and that's saying something.

HIGHLY RECOMMENDED!

EDIT: I'll leave my earlier text as is, but after 1,5 years of polishing it up, I can safely say that AOE4 is also enjoyable.

Base game is decent, This is not Age of Empires, It's a spin off crossover with the sims, the campaigns are not historically accurate (They had a lot of empire exploration material from 1400-1800 AD to use) but decided to make up some random ass stories about love, friendship, inclusivity and life is about learning type of shit. This game..... how to describe this game....

It's not bad by any means, but I think it kinda misses what made age of empires 1 and 2 so good. There's less playable campaign than in age 2, but they are more story driven. They tried to pull a Warcraft 3 and have characters that converse and have a plot. But the plot is just kinda bad, and voice acting worse. I couldn't take anything that was going on seriously.

Gameplay wise, it's fun, but the issue I have is this whole reliance on trading posts, native tribes, and the EXP system. Basically they ask for you to build trading posts, which you can only do in certain locations, and then get food, wood, gold, or EXP from them. Experience points allow you to purchase some upgrades that only you get, which kinda gives you an unfair advantage. On more than one occasion, I was completing the 'finale' mission where it's supposed to be an all-out war, and I ended up just grinding out 3 levels of experience, spending them on free soldiers, then storming the main gate and taking down the objective.

Granted, I was playing on easy mode, but for a game that tries to emulate warcraft 3 a lot, it missed some balancing.

Still very fun and well polished as a strategy game, but I can see why people say that it's the worst of the series. 

6.5/10

I was looking forward to the definitive edition of AoE III and it felt very pleasant.
The nostalgic effect is without a doubt present and combined with the full audiovisual makeover, this gives a breathtaking AoE experience.

I also played the game at 3840 * 1080 resolution and it was fantastic, a comprehensive view of the world gives you a nice advantage of course.
For some this is cheating but I also didn't see myself complaining when I lost to friends at old lan parties with my then 17 "monitor.

AoE III also supports cross platform multiplayer so we can challenge even more players. Spectator mode is also provided.

In addition to the updated graphics, sounds and music, the game brings a number of new things such as 2 new civilizations, 2 new game modes including 1 based on historical battles + accompanying maps.

Whether you are driven to execute strategies or perhaps a relaxing builder, the game has plenty to offer to fulfill your AoE desires.

Despite the devastating news of the DLC cancellation, this game still has a great deal of content. Choose a Nation and Explorer, Build a Deck of Home City shipments that can be called in using experience gathered during the match from Trade Posts and Explorer Actions. Build up to the Imperial Age, or Revolt from your mother-country to become one of the Revolution Nations to drastically change up your strategy mid-game. A significant improvement over the original from 2008, with a wide variety of unique units and upgrades for the player factions, Native sub-factions and Mercenary recruits.

Age of Empires II: Definitive Edition takes everything that made the original a legend and polishes it for the modern era. Crisp 4K visuals, a remastered soundtrack, and a cleaner UI make the game look and feel fresh without losing the soul of the original.

With over 45 civilizations, dozens of historical campaigns, skirmishes, co-op missions, and a thriving multiplayer scene, the replay value is virtually endless. Regular DLC and balance updates keep the game alive and evolving years after release.

Gameplay feels smoother than ever thanks to quality-of-life improvements like smarter villager behavior, better pathfinding, and more intuitive controls. Yet, it still retains the strategic depth and pacing that defined the series. The learning curve can be steep for newcomers, and veteran players may still spot occasional AI quirks, but neither detracts from the overall experience.

Whether you’re a nostalgic veteran or a newcomer discovering it for the first time, this is the way to play Age of Empires II.
